Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The initializer of a evaluates postfix i++: its expression value is the old zero, so a is initialized to zero, while the increment changes i to one. That full expression finishes before the next declaration's initializer begins. The initializer of b therefore obtains old i equal to one and completes the increment to two.

The last statement reads the two saved objects a and b and computes r=0-1=-1. Final values are (a,b,i,r)=(0,1,2,-1). The expression values obtained by postfix increment and the new stored value of i are different records, and both must be tracked.

There is no conflicting unsequenced modification here: the full-expression boundaries provide the required order. The later subtraction performs only reads. Replacing these two initializers by two direct increment arguments would remove that guarantee in C17, rather than preserve the trace as a compact spelling. Conversely reversing the two saved-result statements would change which named argument receives the first old value. Safe rewriting needs both valid sequencing and preservation of the intended value-to-argument mapping.

Question 42. Comma operator inside one argument

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

int i=0;
int r = twice((i++, i+3));

twice(x)=2*x. Find i and r.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The inner parentheses contain one comma-operator expression. Its left operand evaluates i++, producing the old zero as an expression value and changing i to one. The comma operator sequences that entire left evaluation before the right operand, then discards the left value.

The right operand i+3 now reads one and evaluates to four. The value of the comma expression is this right-hand result, so twice receives a single argument four. Its body returns 2·4=8. Final caller i is one and r is eight.

The outer call has one argument, not two: the comma inside the nested parentheses is an operator, while a top-level comma between arguments would be a separator. Confusing the two would change both the call interface and sequencing. In this example no uncertainty remains in the arithmetic because the increment is completed before the read on its right, and all argument work completes before the helper body executes. The discarded zero is not an additional return, argument or hidden caller-side assignment.

Question 43. Return conversion follows expression evaluation

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

double ratio(int a,int b) { return a/b; }

Find ratio(9,4), then propose a corrected fractional implementation.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The parameters a and b are int objects. Consequently the expression a/b uses integer division before the function's double return conversion. At inputs nine and four, it produces quotient two, truncating the positive fractional part. Converting that already computed integer to double gives 2.0. The return type cannot recover the fraction that was lost earlier.

A corrected body can use return (double)a / b;. The cast supplies a floating operand before division, so the other operand is converted for floating division. For these small exactly representable inputs, the result is 2.25. By contrast return (double)(a/b); casts only after the integer quotient was formed and still returns 2.0.

The interface also needs a nonzero denominator. Integer division has additional representability obligations at signed extremes, while a general floating result has its own range and rounding limits. None causes a problem for the stated nine/four example. Follow the conversion chain in order: argument conversion, expression-operand conversion and evaluation, return conversion, then caller-destination conversion. A later wider type does not retroactively change an earlier operation.

Question 44. A missing return value

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

int f(int x){if(x>0)return x;} is called as int y=f(0);. Is y zero?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

At x=0, the condition x>0 is false, so the only displayed return statement is skipped. Execution reaches the ordinary non-void function's closing brace without returning a value. The caller then uses that missing result to initialize y. Under C17 this use gives undefined behavior; no portable numeric value for y follows.

Zero is merely the argument and the false condition's interpretation, not an implicit returned integer. The last expression evaluated inside a function also does not become an automatic result. An explicit value must be supplied on every normally returning path whose result the caller uses.

One possible repair is to return zero after the conditional, if that is the intended specification. Another is a different interface whose remaining path has an explicit effect/error contract. The choice must follow the desired meaning rather than arbitrary compiler output. Falling through the initial invocation of main has a special zero-result rule, but f is not main. The current classification concerns normal fallthrough and a used result; it should not be confused with a path that deliberately never returns.

Question 45. A non-returning branch is not a numeric result

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A helper loops forever for x<0 and returns x*x otherwise. What domain supports a total mathematical function?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The problem stipulates an algorithmic negative-input branch that does not terminate. Under that stipulation, there is no returned integer for x<0. On mathematical integers the nonnegative branch terminates with x2, including result zero at x=0. Restricting inputs to x≥0 therefore makes this a total mathematical function on its stated domain.

For a signed C17 implementation, termination alone is insufficient: the multiplication must also be representable. With maximum int value U, a sufficient exact nonnegative-input range for the square expression is 0≤x≤⌊U⌋. The lower signed bound is irrelevant to its nonnegative result, but the actual multiplication cannot be evaluated outside that range and then retrospectively declared safe.

The divergence stipulation must be respected in real code. A constant while (1) { } is a straightforward C loop expressing an endless branch. C17 permits assuming termination for certain nonconstant controlling expressions whose loops have no specified observable effects; an arbitrary side-effect-free loop cannot be cited without examining that rule. This question's mathematical classification is not a universal claim about every optimized C spelling of a negative-input loop. Failure to return is distinct from returning an unspecified number.

Question 46. Function versus repeated-evaluation macro

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Cambridge Programming in C, Lecture 2 macro family; original comparison

Compare twice(i++) with TWICE(i++) for initially i=3, using the lesson definitions.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Use the explicit definitions: the function twice returns twice its one int parameter; the macro is #define TWICE(x) ((x)+(x)). With initial i=3, calling twice(i++) evaluates the argument once. The argument's expression value is three, and its increment to four completes before the helper body executes. The function therefore returns six and the caller i ends at four.

Textual substitution instead makes TWICE(i++) into ((i++)+(i++)). The two additions' operands both modify i and the addition operator does not sequence one operand before the other in C17. This is undefined behavior, not a legitimate sum of two predictably consecutive old values.

Parenthesizing operands protects syntactic grouping, but does not add sequencing to +. Nor does a function-like macro create a parameter object containing one evaluated input value. The difference is repeated expression substitution versus one argument evaluation followed by use of a parameter. A safely evaluated numeric operand such as an initialized constant can work in both forms, but that limited case does not validate side-effecting arguments. The stated small function computation has no signed-overflow issue.

Question 47. A macro can be defined but surprising

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

#define MAX(a,b) ((a)>(b)?(a):(b))
int i=3;
int r=MAX(i++,2);

Find i and r in C17.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Expand the macro before tracing: the expression becomes ((i++)>(2)?(i++):(2)). Its comparison reads old i=3, schedules the postfix increment and determines that three exceeds two. The conditional operator sequences its first operand before whichever branch is selected, so i has become four before the true branch runs.

The selected i++ now produces the old four as the conditional expression's value and changes i to five. The false branch is not evaluated. Thus r is four and final i is five. Unlike the addition macro in PF 44, the relevant repeated evaluations here are sequenced; the problem is surprising repeated evaluation, not this particular unsequenced-write violation.

The number of evaluations is path-dependent. If initial i were one, the comparison would make it two, the false branch would supply constant two, and no second increment would occur. Balanced parentheses therefore do not establish an evaluate-once interface. Correct macro reasoning expands the tokens, identifies the selected branch and applies that operator's sequencing rules. It should not blindly classify every repeated occurrence of a side-effecting argument in the same way.

Question 48. Default promotions versus prototype conversion

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Contrast a float argument passed to a declared float parameter with one passed as a trailing variadic argument.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

A visible prototype with a float parameter specifies the type of that corresponding parameter. Its argument is converted as if assigned to that parameter, producing a float parameter object. It is not automatically promoted into a double parameter merely because a call boundary is crossed.

A trailing variadic argument is different: no corresponding declared parameter type supplies that conversion. Default argument promotions apply, including float to double and integer promotions for narrow integer types. A variadic implementation must retrieve a value using the type appropriate to those promotions. Fetching a passed double as though it were an unpromoted float is not a harmless representation choice.

Separate the declared fixed arguments before the ellipsis from the trailing arguments after it; one call can contain both conversion regimes. A function without a prototype in historical C17 syntax has further old-style rules and should not be confused with a properly prototyped fixed float parameter. The chapter excludes C23's changed empty-list meaning. Casting the returned result later does not alter the argument conversion or retrieval that has already occurred. The ellipsis also supplies no automatic guarantee that a format string agrees with the promoted values.

Question 49. Printing and returning are separate observations

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

MIT 6.0001 Lecture 4 return/print family; original trace

Python f(x) prints x+1 then returns x*2. With x=4, the caller prints f(x). Give the output and returned value.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Calling f with four first executes its internal print of 4+1=5, so the first output line is 5. That print does not terminate f. The following return computes 4·2=8 and supplies the integer eight as the call's result. The outer print receives that result and writes 8 on the second output line.

The observation is therefore the two-line sequence five, then eight; f's returned value is eight. These are different facts: the first belongs to an output effect, the second to result flow into the caller. The return value of Python's print operation itself is None, but that does not replace f's later explicit return.

If the explicit return were omitted, f would still print five and then fall through, returning None. The outer print would then write None. If the caller merely evaluated f(4) in a script without printing the returned result, the internal five would still appear but a bare returned eight would not automatically be printed as another script output. Recording output events separately from return values prevents all three behaviors from being collapsed into one number.

Question 50. A postcondition too weak for substitution

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

CMU 15-122 Contracts, Exercise 3; independent specification analysis

A helper is specified only to return a positive divisor of positive a,b. May a caller assume it returns gcd(a,b)?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The given postcondition states that the returned r is positive and divides both positive inputs. It does not state that no larger positive common divisor exists. Consider the implementation that always returns one. Since one divides every positive integer, it satisfies exactly that stated guarantee for every permitted pair.

At a=12,b=18, however, the greatest common divisor is six while that implementation returns one. This counterexample proves that the weak contract does not entail a gcd result. It is a logical countermodel to the proposed substitution, not a claim that every implementation with a gcd-like name actually returns one.

A stronger postcondition can state equality to a defined mathematical gcd, or combine common divisibility with a maximality property over other common divisors. The caller may use that stronger statement only after the implementation has been proved to satisfy it. The helper's name and an informal glance into its body do not enlarge a modular specification. Positivity is also essential to the simple always-one example's given domain and to the downward-search proof in PF 49; changing the input domain requires revisiting its boundary cases.

Question 51. An early return still needs the postcondition

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A helper searches candidate divisors d downward and returns as soon as d divides both inputs. What proves it returns the greatest divisor?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Assume positive integer inputs and initialize d to m=min(a,b). Maintain 1≤d≤m and the invariant that every integer c with d<c≤m has already been shown not to divide both inputs. Initially that interval is empty, so the exclusion statement holds without any test.

If the current d divides both, the return branch establishes common divisibility. The invariant excludes every larger candidate up to m, and no positive common divisor can exceed the smaller positive input m. Thus this early return is the greatest common divisor, not merely some divisor.

If d fails and d>1, decrementing it preserves the exclusion invariant: the old d joins the previously excluded interval because its failed test has just ruled it out. The new d remains at least one. When d reaches one, it divides both positive inputs and all larger candidates are excluded, so the final return also satisfies greatestness. The nonnegative variant d−1 decreases on each unsuccessful iteration, proving termination.

The weaker invariant d≥1 proves neither exclusions nor maximality. Likewise decrementing without the failed divisibility test would not preserve the stronger invariant. A caller needs this stronger property stated in the interface if it is to rely on greatestness modularly.

Exact-input visual solution

Divisibility alone proves commonness; the excluded-larger-candidates invariant proves maximality.

Initialize at min(12,18).

Question 52. Summation precondition and a complete invariant

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For triangular(n) in the lesson, state the invariant, result, and safe range at n=100.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Restate the lesson algorithm: for nonnegative n, initialize total=0,k=1; while k≤n, add k to total and increment k; return total. At every guard use 1≤k≤n+1 and total=(k-1)k/2. The initial zero and one satisfy both statements.

If the guard is true at some k, adding k gives (k-1)k/2+k=k(k+1)/2. Incrementing to k'=k+1 therefore restores the formula total=(k'-1)k'/2. At exit, k>n together with k≤n+1 gives k=n+1, hence the returned value is n(n+1)/2.

For n=100, final k is 101 and total is 5050. In fact every input from zero through 100 keeps k between one and 101 and total between zero and 5050, safely within the minimum guaranteed C17 int range. The proof's products describe mathematical values; the loop actually executes small additions and increments. Replacing it with the machine expression n*(n+1)/2 introduces a multiplication that can overflow at larger inputs even when the final mathematical quotient fits. Operation-level safety follows the executed code, not just the final algebraic result.

Question 53. Geometric summation as a helper specification

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

CMU 15-122 Contracts, Exercise 2; mathematical adaptation

Over mathematical integers, a helper returns sum of 2^i for i=0,...,n -1, n>=0. Give a contract and prove its result.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Require an integer n≥0 and specify the mathematical result r=∑i=0n-12i. The empty sum at zero is zero. To prove a closed form, use an accumulator p and index k with 0≤k≤n and p=2k-1 at every loop guard.

Initially k=0,p=0, so p=20-1=0. An iteration adds the next term 2k, producing (2k-1)+2k=2k+1-1. Incrementing k preserves the invariant. On exit k=n, giving the promised result r=2n-1. The remaining-term count n−k decreases, establishing termination for the mathematical loop.

For example, n=4 adds 1,2,4,8 and returns 15. This check illustrates the proof but does not replace its induction. A machine implementation must separately keep every computed power, accumulation and counter update representable. Even evaluation of an asserted closed form such as a machine pow(2,n) can have different bounds from accumulation of powers only through n−1. CMU's C0 modular demonstration and an exact-integer specification must not be transferred unchanged into signed C17 overflow reasoning.

Question 54. Zero exponent is a specification boundary

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

CMU 15-122 Contracts zero-exponent family; original boundary analysis

A power helper initializes r=1,b=x,e=y, loops while e>1, then returns r*b. What fails at y=0?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

At y=0, the original guard e>1 is false immediately. Initial r=1,b=x therefore leads its final r*b expression to return x. The adopted nonnegative-exponent specification instead requires x0=1, including the algorithm's explicit convention 00=1. Except at x=1, the original boundary result is wrong.

A complete mathematical repair is the following exact-integer algorithm; its input exponent is nonnegative:

def power_exact(x, y):
    assert y >= 0
    r, b, e = 1, x, y
    while e > 0:
        if e % 2 == 1:
            r *= b
        e //= 2
        if e > 0:
            b *= b
    return r

At each guard use rbe=xy and e≥0. For old e=2 t>0, the new exponent is t and squaring b preserves the product. For old e=2 t+1, multiplying r by b before reducing/squaring gives (rb)(b2)t=rbe. If t=0, no future base is needed; the returned r already equals the required power. At initial y=0 the body is skipped and r=1 is returned correctly. Each positive e is reduced by integer halving, so termination follows. Translating this mathematical algorithm into fixed-width C still requires safety of each executed multiplication.

Question 55. Unused arithmetic can still overflow

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A repeated-squaring power helper unconditionally squares b on its last loop iteration even when e becomes zero. Is representability of the final mathematical result sufficient?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The question explicitly assumes a32-bit signed int with maximum 2147483647. At x=50000,y=1, the mathematical answer 50000 is representable. A loop iteration may correctly multiply r by b once, yet an unconditional final b*b then computes 2500000000, exceeding that maximum.

The program has executed a signed overflow even if the new base is never subsequently read. A valid final numeric postcondition cannot erase an earlier undefined operation. Safety must cover the whole executed path, including work whose result later becomes dead.

One repair first reduces the exponent and squares only when another exponent bit remains, as in the complete exact-integer algorithm in PF 52. For this example, exponent one becomes zero, the square is skipped and the result 50000 is returned. Another approach checks representability before every multiplication or uses an appropriate checked/wider arithmetic contract. Merely widening the final destination after the int multiplication does not help.

The 32-bit assumption belongs to this example; 50000 need not itself fit every conforming C17 int. Negative bases, exponent zero and signed-range endpoints also need explicit contracts rather than a claim that all representable final powers automatically validate any repeated-squaring implementation.

Question 56. Quotient-remainder uniqueness

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For n=47,d=6, find q,r satisfying n=qd+r and 0<=r<d, then prove uniqueness generally.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

For 47 and positive divisor six, 47=7·6+5, and five is in the required interval from zero through five. Thus q=7,r=5 satisfies both the identity and the remainder bounds.

Suppose two pairs q,r and q2,r2 satisfied n=qd+r=q2d+r2 with positive d and both remainders in [0,d). Subtracting the identities gives (q-q2)d=r2-r. Because the two remainders differ by strictly less than d in magnitude, the right side lies strictly between −d and d. The only multiple of d in that interval is zero. Hence q=q2 and then r=r2.

This proves uniqueness for the mathematical Euclidean specification, including negative n when the specified nonnegative remainder is used. Plain C division on a negative numerator follows a different truncation convention, as PF 55 shows. The stated 47/six case has no such difference.

A two-output implementation must also leave the unique results in the promised distinct output objects. Computing q and r correctly internally does not prove their simultaneous final storage if output aliases overwrite one another. The arithmetic theorem and the program's state/effect contract are separate obligations.

Question 57. Signed division needs a different remainder statement

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

In C17, find q,r for n=-23,d=5. Is 0<=r<d the right contract?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

C17 integer division truncates toward zero. For numerator−23 and divisor five, the quotient is−4. The remainder identity then gives r=-23-(-4)·5=-3. Thus q=−4,r=−3 and -23=(-4)·5+(-3).

The Euclidean condition r≥0 fails for this C result. For defined signed division, a nonzero C remainder has the numerator's sign and magnitude smaller than the divisor's magnitude. Denominator zero and an unrepresentable signed quotient, such as the relevant minimum divided by−1, must be excluded before using this result rule.

With positive divisor d, a negative remainder can be converted to Euclidean form by replacing r by r+d and q by q−1. Here the adjusted pair is q=−5,r=2, and -23=(-5)·5+2. The adjustment preserves the identity and puts the remainder in [0,d); an actual implementation must also justify its arithmetic safety.

Python's // uses floor division and would directly produce−5 for these inputs, so copying its output into a C trace changes the language semantics. Always state whether the contract concerns C truncation or mathematical Euclidean division instead of mixing the quotient from one with the remainder bounds from the other.

Question 58. A frame condition makes replacement reasoning possible

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Two helpers both return x*x. One also increments a global counter. Can a caller substitute either when only the numerical postcondition is stated?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Regard each helper as a transition from an argument and external state to a result and new state. The pure helper maps (x,s) to (x2,s). The stateful one maps (x,s) to (x2,s+1), under their respective termination/arithmetic contracts. Their first components agree, but their second components differ.

If the caller later reads s, the helpers are distinguishable. For example, starting at s=0 and calling once leaves zero or one respectively, despite the same numerical result. A specification stating only result= x2 permits both implementations and therefore cannot support substitution in every state-observing caller.

A frame condition states which external objects may change, or that none relevant to the caller is changed. Together with valid input, termination and the returned relation, it can justify the intended pure abstraction. A name such as square does not supply that condition. Nor does using only the returned value immediately after the call establish that no later observation can reveal an effect. If observations are intentionally restricted to the result, say so explicitly; that is a weaker equivalence claim than interchangeability in arbitrary program contexts.

Question 59. Composing two arithmetic safety conditions

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

f(x)=x+3; g(y)=2*y with C17 int. Derive a sufficient exact input interval for g(f(x)).

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Let L and U be the C17 int limits. The actual input x must lie in [L,U]. The first call computes y=x+3; the second doubles that y. Defined doubling requires L≤2y≤U, hence ⌈L/2⌉≤y≤⌊U/2⌋.

Substitute y=x+3 to obtain the exact interval

x∈[L,U]∩[⌈L2⌉-3,⌊U2⌋-3].

At the lower endpoint, f returns−1073741824 and g returns L. At the upper endpoint, f returns 1073741823 and g returns 2147483646. These inequalities are mathematical reasoning about machine operations, not a request to evaluate a potentially overflowing expression while testing it. The illustrative 32-bit limits are an added example, not an unstated universal assumption about every C17 int.

Question 60. Two callback applications are not one doubled argument

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Find apply(step,4) and its general formula.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

apply first calls the supplied function on four. step computes 3·4-2=10, which is stored in apply's local y. That call has ended before the return expression invokes the callback again, now on ten. The second result is 3·10-2=28, which apply returns.

For general x, the map is T(T(x))=3(3x-2)-2=9x-8. Calling step on twice the original argument instead gives T(2x)=6x-2; at four that is 22, not 28. Repetition of a transformation and transformation of a multiplied input are distinct operations.

The function-pointer parameter contains a copied compatible function-designation value. Copying it does not clone the function's code or make its parameters share caller storage. Each invocation still creates its own ordinary parameter object. The first local assignment and later return expression fix the callback order, so this is not an unspecified-argument-order case. Including apply, there are three helper invocations and at most two simultaneously active helper bodies. Question 61. A stateful callback changes the composition

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A callback step(x) returns x+(++s), with static s initially zero. apply invokes step twice sequentially, passing the first result to the second. Compute apply(step,5).

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Begin with the one persistent counter s=0. The first callback increments it to one, adds that value to its argument five and returns six. The second callback begins with s=1, increments to two, adds two to its argument six and returns eight. The complete apply call therefore returns eight and leaves s=2.

For a general starting counter c and input x, the two sequential returned values are x+c+1 and x+c+1+c+2=x+2c+3. The final counter is c+2. This state-transition formula explains why a later apply on the same input five, starting at c=2, returns 12 and leaves four.

Replacing step globally by the pure function x+1 would predict seven from two applications, which already fails in the first actual call. The callback's history is a hidden input unless the contract exposes it as state. The first result is deliberately fed into the second callback, but the persistent counter is also carried between them; tracking only one of those flows is insufficient. The explicit sequential interface removes call-order ambiguity, and the small stated values avoid signed overflow.

Question 62. Reference and value in the same C++ interface

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Stanford CS 106 B reference family; original mixed-parameter problem

void change(int &x,int y) { x+=y; y=0; }
int a=4,b=7;
change(a,b);

Find final a,b.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

This is C++17, not C17. The reference parameter x binds to the caller's a object, while y is a separate int parameter initialized with the value of b, seven. The statement x+=y reads a=4 and local y=7, then writes 11 into a itself.

Assigning zero to y next changes only that copied parameter object. It does not assign zero to caller b. The final caller values are therefore a=11,b=7; y contains zero just before its invocation ends. Passing an expression as an argument does not by itself determine whether its caller storage is shared: the parameter's declared mode does.

A C pointer interface can achieve access to a caller object too, but requires a pointer declaration, an address argument and an explicit dereference for the write. Its copied pointer parameter is not a C++ reference object that can be explained by silently using this syntax in C. Reference binding also does not imply a fresh copy of a; x is a name designating that caller object throughout its valid binding. No lifetime or overflow issue arises for the given live objects and small values.

Question 63. Two C++ references can designate one object

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

int a=4;

Find a.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Both arguments are the same live caller object a, and both parameters are references. Thus x and y designate that one object rather than two independent int copies. The first statement adds two to a=4, producing six. The next reads the same updated six through y and triples it, producing 18.

The final result is a=18. Reporting distinct outputs six and 12 would incorrectly let y read an independent old four. The common mathematical transition is a↦3(a+2), just as for the sequenced aliased-pointer target case, though the C++ reference syntax is different.

The full statements sequence the two writes, so shared designation is permitted here and is not itself an unsequenced-modification error. A non-aliasing assumption would have to be stated separately; ordinary reference parameters do not guarantee it.

Once x is bound, an assignment such as x=y assigns a value to x's current referent; it does not reseat x to a new object. In this exact alias case such a later assignment would simply copy the same target value to itself. Question 64. A value-result alias requires a copy-out rule

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A theoretical procedure receives two value-result parameters p,q from the same caller x=4. It sets p=10,q=20. Find final x under the two copy-out orders.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The problem stipulates theoretical value-result semantics. Entry copies caller x=4 into two distinct local parameter objects p and q. The body then gives them values 10 and 20. The caller's x is not updated by those local body assignments; effects are copied back at return.

If p is copied out first, x becomes 10, then q's copy-out overwrites it with 20. If q is copied out first, x becomes 20 and p's later copy-out leaves 10. This is neither C value passing nor ordinary immediate C++ reference writes. Matching one final number does not make the semantics equivalent. The two local parameter identities and the shared copy-out destination must both be represented to explain the ambiguity.

Question 65. Call by name re-evaluates an expression

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Under an explicitly defined mathematical call-by-name model, parameter p denotes the caller expression i+1. The body reads p, increments caller i, then reads p again. Initially i=3. Give the two reads and contrast value passing.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Under the explicitly stipulated mathematical call-by-name model, p is a recipe for evaluating the caller expression i+1 in its caller environment. It is not a stored snapshot of the first numerical result. With i initially three, the first read evaluates that recipe to four.

The body then performs the stipulated mutation of the caller's i, making it four. A second read of p evaluates the same expression again in that updated environment, obtaining five. The returned/read pair is therefore (4,5), with caller i finally four.

For call by value, entry evaluates i+1 once to four and stores that value for p. If the body retains its separately stipulated ability to mutate caller i, that mutation still makes i four, but the saved parameter value remains four on both reads. The comparison pair is then (4,4).

This example depends on a theoretical environment-access rule that the question states explicitly. It is not an inference that an ordinary C callee can access any caller local. Nor is the expression i+1 automatically a writable object suitable for a normal non-const C++ int reference. Re-evaluation of an expression, shared access to an object and copied parameter values are three different passing models.

Question 86. A repeated static triangular counter

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A helper adds its argument d to one static s initially zero and returns s. Call with d=1,...,n in separate loop iterations. Derive the sum of all returns.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Let s start at zero and make the sequential helper calls with increments 1,2,...,n. After the kth call, persistent state is the sum of the first k integers, so its returned value is k(k+1)/2. Induction proves this: the previous state (k -1)k/2 plus k equals k(k+1)/2.

The caller sums these returned states, rather than summing only the supplied increments. Its total is

∑k=1nk(k+1)2=12(n(n+1)(2n+1)6+n(n+1)2)=n(n+1)(n+2)6.

At n = 4 the helper returns 1,3,6,10 and the caller total is twenty. The persistent state itself ends at ten, not twenty. State and accumulated returned output are different quantities.

The formulas are mathematical identities. On an explicitly assumed signed int 32 implementation, the triangular state fits through n = 65535, but the sequential sum of returns fits only through n = 2343. The latter gives 2146453540; n = 2344 gives 2149201880, beyond INT_MAX. Evaluating the literal int product n*(n+1)*(n+2) before dividing by six has yet another limit: its numerator already exceeds INT_MAX at n = 1290. Safe final mathematical output does not justify unsafe evaluated intermediates. Later calls also require accounting for any nonzero initial persistent state.

Exact-input visual solution

The two accumulators satisfy triangular and tetrahedral formulas respectively.

Add one to saved and accumulate its returned one.

Question 87. Independent counters versus one shared counter

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Two Python make-counter closures increment by one. One is called twice and the other once, then the first again. Find the four returns and explain storage identities.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Each factory invocation initializes its own n to zero and returns a function that increments and returns that retained binding. Let A be the cell retained by counter a and B the cell retained by counter b. Both begin at zero, but they are distinct cells.

In the stated sequence a(), a(), b(), a(), the first call changes A to one; the second changes A to two; the third changes B to one without changing A; the fourth changes A to three. The returned sequence is therefore [1,2,1,3]. Final retained state is A = 3 and B = 1.

Resetting n on every counter call would instead produce repeated ones, while using one module-wide n would produce [1,2,3,4]. Neither model matches separate factory-created environments. The counter source is shared, but the enclosing state identities are not.

The stem describes the factory in prose, so a test reconstruction must be labelled as a reconstruction rather than the exact printed program. The semantic answer follows directly from the stipulated per-factory binding and increment rule; a diagram should distinguish the two retained cells and highlight only the cell selected by each call.

Exact-input visual solution

Follow the named identity or binding. A local rebinding, shared-object mutation and retained environment update are distinct operations.

factory calls: A = 0; B = 0.

Question 88. A returned reference is not a lifetime cure

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A C++ function returns int& referring to its ordinary automatic local. Does reference syntax keep the local alive?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The ordinary automatic local exists only during its block's lifetime. An int& return can bind a caller reference to that local, but returning from the function ends the local object's lifetime. The caller is then left with a dangling reference and cannot safely read the former integer through it.

The former stored number is not a guaranteed returned value. A particular run appearing to read that number does not establish defined behavior; later storage reuse is only one possible symptom, not the reason the program lacks a valid referent.

This is not C++ lifetime extension for selected temporary-binding contexts. Binding a reference to an ordinary automatic local and returning that reference does not extend the local's lifetime. Nor should the C rule about an indeterminate pointer value be quoted as the definition of every C++ reference rule.

Returning int by value copies the result into the caller's value flow and avoids this dangling-local problem. Returning a reference to a caller-owned object can be valid if that object outlives all uses. Returning a reference to static storage can also preserve lifetime, but introduces shared-state behavior across calls. Each alternative needs its own lifetime and effect contract; changing only the return type spelling cannot supply one.

Question 89. Array parameter size does not recover array length

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A C17 function is declared void f(int a[10]);. Does it receive a copied ten-element array, and can sizeof(a) inside reliably compute ten times sizeof(int)?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

In the C17 parameter declaration void f(int a[10]), a is adjusted to a pointer parameter. The function does not receive a new ten-element array object, and the written ten is not an automatically passed runtime length.

Consequently sizeof a inside the function measures its pointer parameter's type, not ten times sizeof(int). Its numerical size depends on the implementation; neither four nor eight bytes is universally implied. The caller's array object remains where the caller created it, and valid element writes through a can affect that original object.

A length-aware interface must communicate the usable length separately, for example with a size_t parameter and a matching access precondition. The ordinary a[10] syntax should not be confused with the distinct C parameter syntax a[static 10], which explicitly imposes a minimum-access requirement on arguments to calls of that function.

The rule is about parameter adjustment. sizeof on an actual ten-element array object in a scope where its array type is retained is a different expression and does yield ten times its element size. Establish the declaration context before applying a memorized array-size formula.

Question 90. Two expressions with the same value need not be interchangeable

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A pure helper returns 7; another returns 7 but increments global s. A caller evaluates the helper twice and then tests s. Are they interchangeable?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Starting from saved state zero, a pure helper returning seven twice produces returned sequence [7,7] and leaves state zero. A stateful helper that increments saved state before returning the same seven also produces [7,7], but ends at saved state two.

The result sequence is equal while the state transition is different. If callers can later observe that state, replace the helper, or invoke another operation that depends on it, the two implementations are distinguishable. A value-only postcondition is therefore insufficient to justify treating the stateful helper as pure.

Represent the contracts as transformations of both value and state: the pure helper maps state s to returned seven with unchanged s; the other maps s to returned seven with state s+1. Composing two calls gives final s versus s+2. This simple algebra exposes the difference without depending on an implementation's stack layout.

An equivalence argument must first state its observables: return values, permitted external effects, exceptions or failures, and termination as appropriate. If a deliberately restricted observer cannot access the state, a narrower equivalence may be proved under that restriction. It cannot be silently promoted to an unrestricted claim that the helpers behave identically.

Question 91. C++ reference argument alias with a copied value

Original/course-inspired problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

void f(int &a,int b) { a+=b; b+=a; }
int x=3;
f(x,x);

Find final x and local b.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

C++ parameter a is an int reference, so f(x,x) makes a designate the caller's x. Parameter b is passed by value and becomes a separate int initialized to the same original three. Both argument evaluations merely read x, so there is no conflicting argument-side modification to resolve.

The first body statement a += b reads three through a and three from b, then writes six into the caller's x. The second statement b += a reads the updated six through a and adds it to b's still-original three, obtaining local b = 9.

After return, caller x is six. The local b value nine is not copied back and is not a returned result because the function returns void. A correct final report distinguishes the surviving caller value six from the final pre-exit local value nine.

If both parameters were references to x, the second update would instead double the shared six to twelve. If both were values, x would remain three. These comparisons show why argument spelling alone cannot identify the passing model: the declaration determines whether each parameter is a new object or an alias to an existing one.

Exact-input visual solution

Follow the named identity or binding. A local rebinding, shared-object mutation and retained environment update are distinct operations.

entry: a aliases x = 3; b copies 3.

Complete summary and examination rules

Summary. A function definition supplies behavior; a declaration supplies an interface. Each invocation owns distinct parameter objects and automatic locals, while designated static state persists. A call evaluates arguments, initializes parameters, executes its body, and returns to a saved continuation. Scope selects declarations; lifetime determines whether objects still exist; linkage identifies declarations across boundaries. Scalar assignment, pointer reassignment, and target mutation are three different operations. Aliases make sequential mutations share state. Pure functions permit algebraic composition; stateful functions require state composition. Language rules decide whether an output is unique, one of several permitted outcomes, or not defined at all. Contracts connect safe inputs to guaranteed outputs and explicit effects. Python adds object-sharing, lexical closure environments, and definition-time defaults; C++ adds genuine reference parameters.

Examination procedure. (1) State the language and parameter model. (2) Check declarations, call types, initialization, arithmetic range, and pointer lifetime. (3) Give every distinct object an identity, including shared static objects and aliased targets. (4) Separate argument evaluation from parameter initialization. (5) Record pending return continuations. (6) Follow the specified sequencing; branch the trace if order is unspecified. (7) Perform copy-out only if the question explicitly defines such a model. (8) Report the returned result, printed events, and final caller state separately. (9) Verify formulas at zero, one, a boundary, and an alias case. (10) Justify the general relation with contracts or induction; finite runs do not replace a proof.

Interfaces and call execution

Rule 1

A function declaration supplies a type interface; its definition supplies executable behavior. Do not treat a prototype as code that runs or as a complete input-value contract.

Rule 2

Parameter names in compatible prototypes and definitions may differ. Compatibility is about return and parameter types, while names inside an invocation bind its own objects.

Rule 3

Use an explicit void parameter list for a zero-argument C17 prototype. An empty list in a C17 declaration lacks a parameter-type specification; C23 and C++ use different rules.

Rule 4

A visible prototype requires compatible argument types and an appropriate count. A constraint violation requires a diagnostic; it is not a normal arithmetic-output question.

Rule 5

Evaluate an argument expression before binding its resulting value to the parameter. The parameter receives the expression value, not the caller's source-text identifier.

Rule 6

With a prototype, argument conversion occurs as if by assignment to the unqualified parameter type. A narrow type or floating conversion can change the value before the body begins.

Rule 7

A float trailing variadic argument is promoted to double, and narrow integers undergo integer promotions. A variadic interface still requires correctly retrieved promoted types.

Rule 8

The type of a returned expression's arithmetic is determined before return conversion. A double return type cannot recover the fraction already lost by int/int division.

Rule 9

Save a return continuation for every genuinely active call. The continuation records what the caller still needs to do after the callee supplies its result.

Rule 10

Count total invocations and maximum simultaneously active invocations separately. Sequential repeated helpers increase the first count without accumulating live frames.

Rule 11

Nested argument syntax does not automatically imply nested active helper bodies. In f(g(x)), g completes before f's body begins; a call inside f's body is different.

Rule 12

A return transfers control out of the current invocation. A print operation records an output event and normally continues; the two observables must be reported separately.

Rule 13

A void C call cannot supply an integer result. A Python function that falls through returns None; these are different language concepts despite informal “no result” descriptions.

Rule 14

An ordinary non-void C function reaching its closing brace has undefined behavior if the caller uses its result. The zero result for falling through initial main is a specific exception.

Rule 15

A called externally linked function needs an appropriate definition in the program. Missing implementation is a translation/linking issue, not a license to invent runtime values.

Values, identities, and lifetimes

Rule 16

In C, scalar parameters are separate objects initialized with argument values. Assigning such a parameter does not assign the caller's scalar object.

Rule 17

Distinguish the old caller value, the current parameter value, and the returned value in every trace. Equal numerical values do not establish shared object identity.

Rule 18

Discarding a pure helper's returned value leaves caller state unchanged. Assigning that returned value to the caller produces a recurrence that must be traced separately.

Rule 19

For repeated assignments of an affine result T(x)=ax+b, use Tk(x)=akx+b∑j=0k-1aj. Handle a=1 separately when replacing the sum by a quotient.

Rule 20

A mathematical composition may have a stricter domain than its simplified formula. Preserve the preconditions of every inner and outer call even when cancellation removes a denominator.

Rule 21

A parameter object is recreated for each invocation. A recursive call with the same parameter name still owns another object, not the parent's mutable slot.

Rule 22

Scope is visibility of an identifier; storage duration is existence of an object; linkage is identity across declarations. Never use one of these words as a substitute for all three.

Rule 23

Ordinary local variables have block scope. In technical C terminology, function scope belongs to labels, while parameter names in a prototype have prototype scope.

Rule 24

Lexical scope resolves a name using its definition context. An active caller's unrelated local declaration does not become visible in a separately defined C function.

Rule 25

Shadowing introduces a distinct declaration and hides a spelling in a region. It does not delete, overwrite, or merge the outer object.

Rule 26

The scope of a local C declaration begins before its initializer expression. In int x=x, the initializer selects the new uninitialized local, not a hidden outer x.

Rule 27

A new automatic scalar without an initializer is not guaranteed to contain zero. Do not derive an output from guessed previous stack contents.

Rule 28

A block-scope static object is initialized once and persists across calls. Its name remains limited to its block; persistent storage does not imply global visibility.

Rule 29

Distinct static declarations create distinct objects even if their names and initial values match. Conversely, recursive invocations share the single object of one static declaration.

Rule 30

Static-duration objects without explicit initializers receive zero initialization. That guarantee does not extend to ordinary uninitialized automatic objects.

Rule 31

File-scope static gives internal linkage to a function or object. Block-scope static gives static storage duration to an object; it does not define a reference passing mode.

Rule 32

Returning an integer value and returning a pointer to its local object are different operations. The copied value can survive after the automatic object ends.

Rule 33

A returned pointer or C++ reference to an expired automatic local cannot safely access that object. Pointer/reference syntax does not extend its lifetime.

Rule 34

A pointer to a live static object remains usable after return, but later calls can change that shared object. A stable address does not promise a stable value.

Rule 35

Conceptual call-stack diagrams specify identities and continuations. They do not prove a physical stack direction, exact frame size, address, or absence of optimization.

Pointer parameters and aliases

Rule 36

A C pointer parameter receives a copied pointer value. The local pointer object is distinct from the caller's pointer object, although both can designate the same target.

Rule 37

Assignment p=q redirects only the local copied pointer p. Assignment *p=value writes the live designated target, which may be a caller object.

Rule 38

To redirect a caller pointer variable through a parameter, pass the address of that pointer object and write through a compatible pointer-to-pointer.

Rule 39

A pointer's target must exist, be appropriately typed/aligned, and permit the requested access. A non-null value alone does not establish these conditions.

Rule 40

Identify aliases before performing sequential mutations. If p and q designate one object, the second full statement reads the state produced by the first.

Rule 41

The map *p+=2; q=3 gives separate outputs (u+2,3 v) for distinct targets and the single output 3 u+6 for an aliased target. These are different state spaces.

Rule 42

Reversing aliased operations changes their composition unless they commute. Increment-then-scale and scale-then-increment cannot be exchanged without proof.

Rule 43

Temporary-based swapping supports identical valid targets and avoids arithmetic overflow. An arithmetic or XOR replacement needs separate alias and machine-safety analysis.

Rule 44

Multiple output pointers require an explicit alias contract. If two promised final scalar values differ, one scalar object cannot simultaneously retain both.

Rule 45

An output may safely designate an original caller input object when the callee already received the input value by scalar copy. This differs from two outputs aliasing each other.

Rule 46

A pointer member in a copied structure remains a pointer to the original target unless a deep-copy algorithm is explicitly performed. Structure value passing alone does not duplicate reachable objects.

Rule 47

An array-shaped parameter declaration adjusts to a pointer parameter. It neither copies the array nor automatically communicates its runtime length.

Rule 48

sizeof of an adjusted array parameter measures a pointer object, not the caller array. Use an explicit length interface rather than guessing from that expression.

Rule 49

const int * prevents target writes through that pointer access path. It does not establish that no other alias can change the original non-const object.

Rule 50

int *const prevents reassignment of the local pointer but allows valid target writes. const int *const combines two distinct restrictions.

Order, macros, and behavior classification

Rule 51

Commas separating C17 arguments are not comma operators. They do not impose a left-to-right argument evaluation order.

Rule 52

Direct conflicting modifications such as f(i++,i++) are unsequenced in C17 and yield undefined behavior. Do not turn undefined behavior into a small set of plausible answers.

Rule 53

Separate function body executions that are not otherwise ordered are indeterminately sequenced in C17. Two next() calls can complete in either order without interleaving their bodies.

Rule 54

With a counter starting at zero, sub(next(),next()) can return -1 or 1, while add(next(),next()) returns 3 in either permitted order. Unique output does not imply unique internal order.

Rule 55

Separate full expressions can force an order and preserve saved values. When rewriting for clarity, retain which expression value is saved before each side effect.

Rule 56

The actual comma operator sequences its left operand before its right operand and yields the right operand's value. Parentheses can distinguish it from argument punctuation.

Rule 57

C && and || sequence and conditionally evaluate operands. Their control effects can skip a call entirely, so call counts must include short-circuit conditions.

Rule 58

Signed arithmetic outside the representable range is undefined in C. Do not import C0's modular integer interpretation from a contracts example into signed C code.

Rule 59

Mathematical representability of the final result is insufficient. With an explicitly assumed int 32, 50000 raised to exponent one fits, but an unused square of 50000 is 2500000000 and overflows. Check every executed intermediate and avoid a final square that the algorithm never needs.

Rule 60

A function-like macro substitutes tokens rather than creating parameter objects. Expand it before analyzing value, side effects, precedence, or scope.

Rule 61

Parentheses around macro parameters fix many precedence errors but do not guarantee one evaluation. TWICE(i++) still performs two unsequenced modifications under addition.

Rule 62

A conditional macro can evaluate an argument twice with defined sequencing. MAX(i++,2) at i=3 produces result 4 and final i=5; “repeated” is not automatically “unsequenced.”

Rule 63

Classify language constraints, undefined behavior, unspecified outcomes, implementation-defined choices, and ordinary defined execution before deriving an output. These classifications are not interchangeable.

Rule 64

C++17 argument sequencing rules differ from C17. A similar-looking C++ expression must receive its own language label and analysis.

Contracts, callbacks, and cross-language distinctions

Rule 65

A precondition is an obligation at the call site. A postcondition may be used after a safe normal return; total correctness additionally requires termination.

Rule 66

A frame condition limits which external objects may change. A numerical postcondition alone does not prove that a helper is pure.

Rule 67

A specification promising a positive common divisor does not promise the greatest common divisor. For inputs twelve and eighteen, returning one meets the weaker contract but misses the gcd six. A descending search proves greatestness by maintaining that every larger candidate has already failed, not merely by testing that the current candidate divides both inputs.

Rule 68

Every reachable return site must establish the postcondition, including early returns inside a loop. A proof only for the closing return is incomplete.

Rule 69

To compose helpers, establish each next call's precondition from previous postconditions and preserved state. Safe individual helpers do not make all caller arithmetic safe.

Rule 70

Quotient/remainder contracts require a defined division domain, a remainder convention, and valid distinct outputs when both values must survive. In C, negative division truncates toward zero.

Rule 71

A callback's callable type must match its implementation. An incompatible cast does not turn one function signature into another valid calling convention.

Rule 72

Pure callback composition permits algebraic substitution; stateful callback composition must include changing state. A callback called twice can use two different persistent counter values.

Rule 73

A C++ reference parameter aliases its referent; a value parameter copies its value. Passing the same argument twice can therefore produce one alias and one copy.

Rule 74

C++ assignment through a reference changes its referent; it does not reseat the reference. Binding restrictions and referent lifetime still apply.

Rule 75

Value-result and call-by-name are theoretical passing models unless the question supplies a language supporting them. Value-result aliases need a copy-out order to define a unique final state.

Rule 76

Python parameters bind to supplied objects. Rebinding a local name does not rebind a caller name, while mutating a shared mutable object can be visible through both.

Rule 77

Python free variables follow lexical parents, not the current caller. Returned closures can retain their enclosing bindings after the factory call finishes.

Rule 78

Python defaults are evaluated when the definition executes. A mutable default is shared across calls using it; an explicit argument does not reset that stored default.

Rule 79

Loop-created Python closures can share a late-read binding: saved functions reading i after range(3) can all return two. A definition lambda i=i: i instead saves defaults zero, one and two at the respective definitions. Its parameter can still be overridden by an explicit call argument; saving a mutable default would not create a deep copy.

Rule 80

A Python binding operation can make a name local throughout its function block, causing an earlier read to raise UnboundLocalError. State session/error outcomes accurately; a failed call does not supply a normal numeric return.

Exact call-state laboratory

The laboratory replays curated, defined models with an adjustable integer input. It does not execute arbitrary submitted code or assign outputs to undefined expressions. Each checkpoint records the caller state, active local state, shared-object state, returned result, and pending continuation. Argument tokens move into a callee and returned tokens move back to the caller; the original caller object remains in place. Choose scalar copying, pointer mutation, aliased updates, static persistence, or nested calls and compare their exact formulas. Playback begins paused. The conceptual stack does not impose any physical address layout or promise that a compiler allocates visible frames.

Static model: each of three calls resets fresh to zero, increments it, adds the input to saved (initially zero), and returns 10 × fresh + saved. Negative inputs are valid for every listed nonrecursive model. Laboratory transitions are integer-exact and begin paused.

Its source audit names all six reviewed candidates and the exact written portions; it does not certify an exhaustive global course search.
